rv.q: Overall this is a beautiful piece, and throughout there’s a playful yet provocative use of theatre.

Irish avant-garde theatre company Dead Centre and British Sign Language (BSL) poet Zoë McWhinney have collaborated to create an experimental epic of war and resistance that'll make you rub your eyes and reach desperately for something real to hold on to.
Through judicious use of a camera lens there is an intermittent telescoping effect in which what we see is rendered both very small and very large.
Deaf Republic is a ravishing and unnerving play about deafness, occupation, resistance, puppets and things that hover outside the edge of comprehension.
At times, Deaf Republic has more of the static quality of an art installation.
The story’s central couple (warmly played by Romel Belcher and Caoimhe Coburn Gray) are beguiling guides, often appearing in marionette form.
Deaf Republic is a marvel of a show.
It’s a brilliant showcase of what theatre can do, and a beautiful story of resilience, performed with spectacular creativity.
Moving in its contemporary relevance, Deaf Republic also has a dramatic exuberance and a touching humanity.
McWhinney and Dead Centre are so effective at pulling us into the story that it feels more real than we care to admit.

This scene is stunningly choreographed in silence, as the gathered townspeople express their horror at what has taken place as they’re one by one driven from the square, leaving just Sonya cradling the dead child (in puppet form).
Is it entertaining? Yes, in many respects, but not to the degree that you would rave about it as a 'must see'.
Serious intent is compromised by the urge to entertain, to create a fun show.
It opens a portal into the kind of theatrical experience that is increasingly rare.
Deaf Republic is innovative, informative and impressive.
Deaf Republic is a seriously impressive play – one which offers its audience the possibility to imagine different normalities and make change.
Deaf Republic is invigorating and passionate theatre which succeeds on a majority of levels.
Its claustrophobia overwhelms and moves, whilst leaving Dead Centre room for yet another slant on Ilya Kaminsky’s imaginary.

cn.t: Critics largely praise this inventive adaptation of Kaminsky's poems for its visceral, multi-layered storytelling using puppetry, BSL, and video, though some find it laborious. The production's experimental approach divides opinion.
